chapters.title: Chapter 3: Constructing and Testing a Factor Strategy

lessons.title: Portfolio Construction: Long-Only vs Long-Short, Rebalancing Frequency

body.text: A ranked list of stocks is not a portfolio. Two quants with the identical factor score can build completely different strategies depending on just two decisions: whether to short the bottom of the ranking or simply avoid it, and how often to act on a score that is already starting to go stale the moment it is calculated.

children.text: Chapter 1 briefly introduced long-only versus long-short as one of five mechanical construction choices. This lesson treats it as what it actually is for an Indian quant, a decision shaped as much by market infrastructure, securities lending, derivatives eligibility, as by pure strategy design, alongside the equally consequential question of how often to rebalance.
Long-Only vs Long-Short: What You're Actually Choosing

A long-only factor strategy simply overweights or exclusively holds the top-ranked bucket of stocks; the bottom of the ranking is never owned, but never actively bet against either. A long-short strategy goes further, taking a short position in the bottom-ranked bucket alongside the long position in the top bucket, which, done correctly, largely cancels out the portfolio's exposure to the broad market and isolates something much closer to the pure factor premium itself, since both legs move with the market but the long-short spread mostly reflects the factor being ranked on. The trade-off is operational complexity: shorting requires infrastructure that simply holding stocks does not.
STT, SLBM, and F&O Eligibility: India's Shorting Constraints

markDefs.definition: The official framework allowing market participants to borrow shares, for a fee, in order to sell them short and later return them, distinct from simply carrying an unsettled short position.

children.text: This is where an Indian quant analyst runs into a constraint a US-trained textbook rarely mentions. In the NSE cash market, a retail trader cannot simply carry a short position in an individual stock overnight without formally borrowing the shares through India's

, or SLBM, an operationally involved process generally used by institutional participants rather than individual traders. Beyond that, genuine multi-day short exposure to a stock is most commonly built using equity derivatives, futures and options, and SEBI and NSE only permit derivatives trading on a specific, periodically reviewed list of stocks that meet defined market capitalisation and liquidity criteria. A large share of the smallcap and microcap universe, exactly the segment a naive bottom-decile short in a size or value strategy might target, simply has no listed futures or options contract available to short at all.

This structural gap is why many systematic strategies in India that want market-neutral exposure do not attempt to short the individual bottom-decile stocks at all. Instead, they hold the long-only top-decile portfolio and hedge out its overall market exposure using Nifty or Bank Nifty index futures, a 'long stock portfolio, short index futures' construction that approximates a market-neutral factor exposure without ever needing to short an illiquid, F&O-ineligible smallcap directly.

body.text: In US-centric factor investing literature, long-short is often presented as the default, cleanest way to isolate a factor. In India, long-only with an index futures overlay is frequently the more practical default, not because long-short is theoretically inferior, but because the bottom decile of most factor rankings sits outside the F&O-eligible universe entirely, making a genuine single-stock short simply unavailable.

children.text: Rebalancing Frequency: The Turnover vs Signal Decay Trade-off

Every rebalance costs money, brokerage, STT, and market impact from Chapter 3's earlier lesson, and every day between rebalances lets the factor score go stale as prices and fundamentals move. Different factors decay at different speeds, which is exactly why NSE's own factor indices do not all rebalance on the same schedule. A momentum score, built on recent price action, can shift meaningfully within weeks, favouring more frequent rebalancing despite the higher turnover cost. A value or quality score, built on fundamentals like P/E or ROE that only update with each quarterly result, changes far more slowly, so rebalancing too often mostly just churns the portfolio and pays transaction costs without capturing any genuinely new information.

body.caption: Illustrative turnover cost drag by rebalancing frequency (hypothetical assumptions, not a real strategy's results)

children.text: The pattern in that table is the whole argument in miniature: momentum's faster-decaying signal justifies its higher turnover cost, because rebalancing less often would mean holding increasingly stale winners and losers, while value's slower-moving signal means frequent rebalancing would mostly just add cost without adding insight. The right frequency is not a universal constant, it is a trade-off specific to how fast each factor's underlying signal actually changes.

Chapter 3's first lesson introduced equal weighting and score-proportional weighting for stocks that clear the breakpoint. A third approach, risk parity, or inverse-volatility weighting, sizes each position so it contributes roughly equal risk to the portfolio rather than equal capital, giving less rupee exposure to a stock's more volatile names and more to steadier ones.

body.title: Designing a Market-Neutral Momentum Strategy
body.scenario: A prop trading applicant wants to build a market-neutral momentum strategy across the Nifty 500 universe, long the top decile by 12-1 momentum and short the bottom decile, rebalanced monthly. While researching implementation, they discover that a large portion of the bottom-decile stocks in a typical month are smallcap names with no listed futures or options contract on the NSE.
body.prompt: Given the constraints covered in this lesson, what is the practical problem with the original design, and what is a workable alternative that still targets a broadly market-neutral outcome?
body.modelAnswer: The practical problem is that many bottom-decile stocks, especially smaller, less liquid names, are not F&O-eligible, so there is no straightforward way to actually short them, and SLBM-based stock borrowing for a large, frequently rotating basket of names is operationally heavy and not readily accessible to most traders. A workable alternative is to run the strategy long-only on the top-decile momentum basket and hedge the resulting market exposure using Nifty or Bank Nifty index futures instead of shorting the bottom decile directly. This does not perfectly replicate a pure long-short momentum factor, since it removes market beta rather than isolating the momentum spread exactly, but it is implementable within India's actual derivatives eligibility constraints, which a textbook-perfect long-short design is not.

body.title: Test Yourself: Matching Rebalancing to Signal Speed
body.question: Why do momentum strategies typically rebalance more frequently than value strategies, despite the higher resulting transaction costs?
options: Momentum strategies are required by SEBI to rebalance monthly
Momentum signals, based on recent price action, decay faster than value signals, based on slower-moving fundamentals, so infrequent rebalancing would mean holding increasingly stale rankings
There is no real difference; all factors should rebalance on the same schedule for consistency
Value strategies actually rebalance more frequently than momentum strategies
body.explanation: Momentum is built on recent price action, which can shift meaningfully within weeks, so the signal decays quickly and justifies more frequent rebalancing despite higher turnover costs. Value and quality signals, built on slower-moving fundamentals like P/E or ROE, stay relevant longer, so less frequent rebalancing captures nearly the same information at a lower cost.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: India's official framework allowing market participants to borrow shares, for a fee, in order to sell them short and later return them.

The SEBI- and NSE-defined, periodically reviewed list of stocks permitted for derivatives (futures and options) trading; many smaller NSE-listed stocks are not on this list, limiting how they can be shorted.
Hedging a long-only stock portfolio's market exposure by shorting Nifty or Bank Nifty index futures, an alternative to shorting individual stocks directly when many of them are not F&O-eligible.
A position-sizing approach that allocates capital inversely to each holding's own volatility, so each position contributes roughly equal risk to the portfolio rather than equal rupee capital.

body.text: Turnover and cost figures in this lesson's table are hypothetical assumptions used purely to illustrate the trade-off between rebalancing frequency and transaction costs, not the actual historical results of any real strategy. F&O eligibility criteria and SLBM rules are set and periodically revised by SEBI and NSE; always verify current rules directly before relying on them.

points: Long-only strategies simply avoid the bottom-ranked bucket; long-short strategies actively short it to isolate a purer factor return, at the cost of significant operational complexity
India's SLBM framework and SEBI/NSE's limited F&O-eligible stock list make single-stock shorting of the full universe, especially smallcaps, impractical for many systematic strategies
A common Indian workaround is holding a long-only factor portfolio and hedging market exposure with Nifty or Bank Nifty index futures rather than shorting individual bottom-decile stocks
Rebalancing frequency should match how fast each factor's signal decays: momentum typically needs more frequent rebalancing than value or quality despite higher turnover costs
Turnover cost drag compounds across rebalances, so a strategy's optimal frequency balances signal freshness against cumulative transaction costs

Equal weight, score-proportional, and risk-parity (inverse-volatility) weighting are three distinct position-sizing approaches, each trading off simplicity, conviction, and risk concentration differently
